clock 0:15: reads the opponent's Hero Giant ability as an elixir trap and refuses it — "He's going to go for the giant ability, but because he goes for the ability, then we can just go for the E-Barbs. He was hoping that we would ability so then we wouldn't have any elixir for defense."

clock 0:03: grades the opponent's last Giant as a cycle mistake, not a placement one — "I knew that he went for a bad giant cuz he didn't have his dark prince back in cycle yet and that's like his main defense."
dark-prince: clock 0:03: named as the opposing Giant deck's key defensive card and the reason its last push failed — "he didn't have his dark prince back in cycle yet and that's like his main defense." Never labelled by the detector; identified from commentary only.

bullets: Game 5 of 8 in a single-deck session; a win against a Hero Giant / Prince / Dark Prince beatdown deck, taking the enemy right tower at clock 0:21 and holding his own left tower at 2667 HP — "GG's. A very nice win" (clock 0:03).

The deck is piloted as bridge pressure, not as beatdown: two of three Rune Giants go straight to a bridge tile ((1, 14) at clock 2:37, (15, 13) at clock 0:39) and only one is built from the back ((8, 0) at clock 1:45). His stated rule is "if we can win the bridge battle like that, it's usually going to reward us pretty nicely" (clock ~1:57).

Rune Giant + Evo Elite Barbarians is the core interaction, and the enchant target is chosen deliberately — "I'm going to boost my E-Barbs with the Rune Giant right away this time. Last time I boosted the Mother Witch first" (clock 1:35), with the Elite Barbarians dropped onto the walking Rune Giant at (7, 10) rather than behind it.

Berserker (Hero) is treated as an elixir resource: deployed four times but Savage Survival fired only once, at clock 0:42 on a defensive Berserker at (9, 9). He explicitly declines it at clock 2:25 ("I don't think we're going to need it actually") and wins the game by refusing to trade abilities with the opponent's Hero Giant at clock 0:15.

Heal Spirit and Minions are the push sustainers, Zap and Fireball the finishers: the enemy right tower is taken from 4406 to zero between clock 0:59 and clock 0:21 by Elite Barbarians + Rune Giant pressure, a Fireball on the defenders (clock 0:27) and an Evo Zap timed off the enemy tower troop's ammo (clock 0:22).

He is explicit that the list loses a straight defensive fight to a real Giant deck and plans around it — "his Giant has more HP than the Rune Giant, which is scary ... We're just going to have to get like one or two good counter pushes that end up taking his whole tower cuz we're probably not going to be able to hold on for the entire game" (clock 1:19-1:07).

new_deck.rationale: A 3.25 average-elixir list with no support building whose Rune Giant and Evo Elite Barbarians are placed at the bridge as punishes far more often than they are built from the back, which is bridge-spam behaviour with a beatdown tank.
new_deck.why_it_works_md: The Rune Giant is only 4 Elixir, so this list can lead with a tank at the bridge instead of saving up behind the King Tower, and her enchant turns the fast-hitting cards around her into real damage. Evolved Elite Barbarians are the intended enchant target and Ryley places them onto the walking Rune Giant so the throw lands immediately ("I'm going to boost my E-Barbs with the Rune Giant right away this time", clock 1:35). Berserker as a Hero gives the deck a 2 Elixir defender that doubles as a 5 Elixir burst when Savage Survival is worth spending, and Ryley's discipline about *not* spending it is what wins this match. Heal Spirit and Minions keep a committed push alive, while Evo Zap and Fireball convert the surviving pressure into tower HP. The weakness he states himself is defence: a real Giant out-tanks the Rune Giant, so the deck has to race rather than hold.
